metaDescription: Six Hawkins stovetop pressure cookers compared by size, aluminium vs hard anodised vs stainless, and induction fit, with an honest read on upkeep and parts.
expertTake: The Hawkins 5 Litre Contura in stainless steel is the best all-rounder because it works on induction and never needs recoating. The Classic CL40 in plain aluminium is the value pick for gas stoves and everyday dal, rice and curry. Anyone who wants a push-button electric machine with presets should skip this category and buy an electric multicooker instead.
introParagraphs: A stovetop pressure cooker with an inner lid is one of the simplest sealed vessels in a kitchen. The lid sits inside the pot, steam pressure pushes it tighter against a rubber gasket, and a weighted regulator on top lets excess steam escape at a set pressure. There are few parts, nothing electronic, and almost nothing to fail.

That simplicity is why this design is still common in many households. Choosing well comes down to three things: the capacity you really cook, the pot metal, and whether your hob is gas, electric coil or induction. This guide walks through the range from small aluminium pots to thick-bottom stainless, using spec data and standard engineering knowledge.

products.name: Hawkins 5 Litre Contura Stainless Steel Pressure Cooker
products.description:
This is the most versatile Hawkins in the range. The body and lid are stainless steel, with a thick sandwich base listed at 6.6 mm that spreads heat and keeps the bottom flat. That base is what makes it behave on induction, where a thin warped base would heat unevenly or fail to register on the hob.

The tradeoff is weight and price compared with plain aluminium. Stainless is also harder to keep from sticking on a dry sauté of onions, so a splash of oil or water at the start helps. Next to the 4 litre stainless Hss40 it simply offers more volume, and next to the Contura 3 litre it suits a family rather than a couple.

Ownership is easy. Wash the lid and gasket after use, keep the vent clear and replace the rubber gasket when it hardens, usually every year or two with regular use. Stainless will not pit or discolor the way thin aluminium can with acidic foods, so it is the choice if you cook tomato or tamarind dishes often.
products.bestFor: Families cooking on induction or mixed hobs who want a durable, uncoated pot.
pros: Stainless body and lid with no coating to wear
Thick sandwich base suits induction hobs
5 litre size feeds five to seven people
Resists pitting from acidic foods
cons: Food sticks without a little oil
Rubber gasket still needs periodic replacement

products.name: Hawkins 4 Litre Stainless Steel Pressure Cooker Hss40
products.description:
The Hss40 uses food-grade 18/8 stainless for both body and lid, and the listing stresses an extra-thick sandwich bottom that stays flat and heats evenly. The lid fits inside the pot, so pressure helps keep it sealed. For a household of four it is a sensible size, enough for rice and dal at once without crowding.

The weakness is that it sits between two better-defined choices. If you cook for two, the 3 litre Contura is lighter and faster. If you cook for six, the 5 litre Contura is roomier. It also costs more than the aluminium Classic CL40 of the same capacity, so the extra money buys induction support and corrosion resistance rather than faster cooking.

In year three expect the gasket to be the only wear item, plus a possible safety valve if it ever blows out. Keep a spare gasket in a drawer, wash the lid vent each time and store with the lid inverted so the rubber does not stay compressed. It is a good one-pot kitchen workhorse.
products.bestFor: Four-person households that want stainless durability without going to 5 litres.
pros: 18/8 stainless resists staining and pitting
Extra-thick base heats evenly and stays flat
4 litre size suits four to six people
Works on gas, electric and induction
cons: Not as roomy as the 5 litre Contura
Sticks if used with too little liquid

products.name: Hawkins 4 Litre Classic Aluminium Pressure Cooker CL40
products.description:
The CL40 is the classic Hawkins: a polished aluminium pot with an inner lid and a base listed between 3.25 and 4.06 mm thick. Aluminium conducts heat quickly, so pressure builds fast on a gas flame and the cooker is light to lift. For everyday rice, lentils and curries at four to six servings, it is hard to fault.

The tradeoff is material. Bare aluminium can darken with acidic or salty foods and should not go in a dishwasher. It is also not made for induction hobs, which need a magnetic base, so check your stove before buying. Compared with the stainless Hss40, you give up induction and long-term shine in return for a lower purchase price and lower weight.

Ownership is routine: wash by hand, dry the lid, store with the gasket relaxed and inspect the vent pipe for blockage. A spare gasket and safety valve cost little and are widely sold. This is the pot to choose if you use gas and want the lowest cost per litre.
products.bestFor: Gas-stove cooks who want a light, quick and low-cost everyday pot.
pros: Light and heats fast on gas flames
Base thickness listed at 3.25 to 4.06 mm
Inner lid design uses steam to hold the seal
Lowest cost per litre in the Hawkins range
cons: Aluminium can darken with acidic food

products.name: Hawkins 5 Litre Classic Aluminium Pressure Cooker CL50
products.description:
The CL50 is the 5 litre sibling of the CL40 and uses the same virgin aluminium body and polished finish. The listing rates it for five to seven people, which makes it the usual choice for a family that cooks a full pot of dal or biryani at once. Because it is aluminium, it is lighter than the stainless 5 litre Contura.

Its compromise is the same as the CL40: no induction, and the metal wants gentle handling. At five litres, a full pot of liquid is heavy to move, so lift it carefully and never fill past two thirds. Compared with the 10 litre Classic, it is the larger size that still fits normal cabinets.

Ownership is simple. Keep the gasket and vent clean, replace the gasket when it softens or the cooker leaks steam from the rim, and avoid scouring the interior. If you move to induction later, you will need to buy a different cooker.
products.bestFor: Larger families on gas who want one pot for big batches.
pros: 5 litre capacity for five to seven people
Aluminium keeps weight lower than stainless
Same dependable inner lid design as other Classics
Spare gaskets and valves are widely sold

products.name: Hawkins 3 Litre Contura Black Hard Anodised Pressure Cooker CB30
products.description:
The CB30 pairs a hard anodised body with a stainless steel lid. Anodising hardens the surface, and the black body heats quickly. It is more scratch resistant than bare aluminium and easier to wipe clean, which is why it appeals to cooks who stir and scrape a lot.

The limits are capacity and hob type. Three litres suits three or four people and is less forgiving for a big pot of beans, which should only fill half the pot. Compared with the induction-compatible 3 litre Contura listed in the same family, the plain CB30 is the version for gas and radiant hobs.

Expect to wash by hand to protect the finish, keep the gasket supple and replace it periodically. The black exterior hides stains, but check the lid underside for residue. It is the pick if you want a smaller pot with a tougher surface than plain aluminium.
products.bestFor: Couples and small families on gas who want a tougher surface than bare aluminium.
pros: Hard anodised body resists scratching
Stainless steel lid is easy to keep clean
Curved body makes stirring easier
Black body heats quickly

products.name: Hawkins 2 Litre Classic Aluminium Pressure Cooker CL20
products.description:
The CL20 is the smallest practical choice for a couple. It follows the Classic recipe: aluminium body, inner lid, rubber gasket and weighted regulator. Small pots build pressure quickly and use little fuel, so a pot of rice or a small batch of lentils is done fast.

Capacity is the whole story. Two litres leaves about one and a third litres of working volume, enough for dinner for two and a side, but not for batch cooking. Next to the 1.5 litre Classic it is slightly more flexible, and next to the 3 litre Contura it is lighter and lower in cost.

Ownership is light. A small pot is simple to wash and store, though the gasket and vent need the same care as a big cooker. Many households buy one as a second pot for quick tasks, and that is where it earns its place.
products.bestFor: Couples, single cooks and second-pot duty for small batches.
pros: Compact and light for small kitchens
Pressure builds quickly in a small volume
Same inner lid safety design as larger models
Lowest fuel use of the group
cons: Only about one and a third litres of working volume

buyingCriteria.criterion: Pot metal: aluminium, anodised or stainless
buyingCriteria.explanation: Aluminium like the Classic CL40 and CL50 is light and heats fast but can darken with acidic foods. Hard anodised, as in the CB30, is tougher but still aluminium underneath. Stainless as in the 5 litre Contura and Hss40 is heavy and durable and the one that works on induction. Choose by your hob first, then by how much you cook acidic dishes.

Induction needs a magnetic base, and thin aluminium does not provide one. The 5 litre Contura stainless and the Hss40 list thick sandwich bottoms, so they suit induction. The Classic CL40, CL50 and CL20 are meant for gas and radiant hobs. Many buyers get this wrong when upgrading a kitchen, so check before buying.

Hawkins rates the CL20 for two or three people, the CB30 for three or four, the CL40 for four to six and the CL50 for five to seven. Never fill beyond two thirds, and only half for beans and rice. Buy for your regular dinner, not for a party, and add a second small pot rather than one huge one.

An inner lid means the lid sits inside the pot and steam pressure presses it against the gasket, so it cannot open under pressure. A weighted regulator vents excess steam at a set level, and a safety valve acts as a backup. Keep the vent pipe clear; a blocked vent is the one real hazard. Check the rubber gasket for hardening every few months.

A thick base spreads heat and resists warping. The Classic range lists a base of 3.25 to 4.06 mm, the Contura extra-thick induction model lists 4.88 mm, and the 5 litre stainless lists 6.6 mm. A warped base on induction can wobble and cook unevenly. Do not quench a hot pot in cold water, which causes warping.

Gaskets, safety valves and regulators are wear items on every stovetop cooker. Hawkins parts are widely sold and cost little, so budget a gasket every year or two. A cooker is only as safe as its gasket and vent. Buy genuine parts that match the model and size, since a gasket for a 5 litre pot will not seal a 3 litre pot.

howWeEvaluated.title: Material and heat handling
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared aluminium, hard anodised and stainless bodies and their listed base thickness. The 5 litre Contura stands out at 6.6 mm, while the Classics list 3.25 to 4.06 mm.

howWeEvaluated.title: Hob compatibility

cards.label: Aluminium (CL20, CL40, CL50)
cards.text: Light, quick to heat and low in cost, with the classic Hawkins performance. It can darken with acidic foods and does not work on induction.

cards.label: Stainless (5 Litre Contura, Hss40)
cards.text: Heavier and costlier but durable, resistant to pitting and compatible with induction. Food sticks more without oil.

howToChoose.note: Pick aluminium for gas and lowest cost, stainless for induction or acidic cooking.

howToChoose.subheading: For Daily Dal and Rice Specifically

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A pot sized so beans and rice fill no more than half, a regulator that vents steadily and a base that does not scorch lentils. Foamy foods need the extra headroom.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The 4 litre Classic CL40 handles daily dal and rice for a family of four, and the 5 litre CL50 gives more headroom for beans.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You cook on induction or make acidic foods daily. The 5 litre Contura stainless and the Hss40 pay back in durability.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You cook on gas and want a straightforward family pot. The Classic CL40 or CL50 does the job at the lowest cost.

maintenance.why: Rubber hardens and stretches with heat, causing steam leaks at the rim. A fresh gasket restores the seal.
Food particles can block the vent, which is the main hazard in a stovetop cooker. A pin or thin brush clears it.
The valve is a backup in case the regulator clogs. If it looks deformed or leaks, replace it.

maintenance.task: Hand wash and dry the lid
maintenance.why: Dishwashers dull aluminium and anodised finishes. Drying prevents water spots and odor.
Leaving the lid sealed traps odor and compresses the gasket. Inverting it lets the rubber relax.

faq.a: The 5 litre Contura stainless, the 4 litre stainless Hss40 and the extra-thick Contura listing mention induction compatibility. The aluminium Classic range is intended for gas and radiant hobs.

faq.q: Is aluminium safe to cook in?
faq.a: Aluminium cookware is widely used and many cooks prefer it for heat response. Acidic foods can discolor it, and stainless is the option if that bothers you.
Match the pot to your usual dinner and fill it no more than two thirds. A 4 litre pot suits four to six people, and 5 litres suits larger families.

faq.q: How often should I replace the gasket?
faq.a: Plan on every 12 to 24 months with regular use, sooner if steam leaks from the lid edge. Always use the gasket made for your pot size.

faq.q: Can I use it for canning?
faq.a: No. Home canning needs a purpose-built canner with a gauge, and these cookers are not approved for it.

faq.q: Is it safe to open right after cooking?
faq.a: Wait until pressure has dropped and the regulator has stopped venting. The inner lid will not release while pressure remains.
